title: "Loosen my tongue"
hook: Musa asks for an open chest, an easy task, a loosened tongue, and his brother Harun as help

segments.voice: Yesterday: the staff and the shining hand, two signs made from what Musa already held. Your line was what's in your right hand? Did you use it on purpose? Day fifty.

Think of the thing you dread most. Maybe it's a phone call. A presentation. Telling your parents something. Walking into a room where someone is angry with you. Your chest goes tight, your mouth goes dry, and the words you practiced disappear. Now Musa gets his assignment: go to Pharaoh. He has transgressed. The man whose house you grew up in. The man whose people you ran from, with a death on your hands. Go and talk to him. Musa doesn't say no. He doesn't pretend he's fine either. He asks for help, very specifically, in four parts. Today: loosen my tongue.
screen: `THE THING YOU DREAD.` → `GO TO PHARAOH.` → `HE ASKS FOR HELP.`

segments.voice: Surah Ta-Ha. Rabbi ishrah li sadri. My Lord, expand my chest for me. Then: make my task easy for me. Then: untie the knot from my tongue, so they understand what I say. Then: give me a helper from my family, Harun, my brother. Strengthen me through him, and let him share my task. Look at the order. He starts inside, with the chest, the place where fear sits and squeezes. Expand it. Give me room to breathe. Then the task itself. Then the words. Then a person. He doesn't ask for the task to go away. He asks to be made big enough for it. That first line is one of the best-known prayers in Islam. Many Muslims say it before exams, job interviews, a hard conversation, a speech. Students write it at the top of their notes. The knot on his tongue: the Qur'an doesn't say what it was. There's a well-known story that as a baby in Pharaoh's palace Musa put a burning coal in his mouth, and it left him slow of speech. That story comes from the commentaries, not the Qur'an, so take it as a story people tell. The text says only that there was a knot, and that he asked for it to be untied. And the helper. The word is wazir, one who carries a burden with you. It's where the English word vizier comes from. Musa asks for his brother, so he doesn't have to walk into that palace alone. A few verses later comes the answer: you have been granted your request, O Musa.
screen: `EXPAND MY CHEST.` · `MAKE MY TASK EASY.` · `UNTIE THE KNOT FROM MY TONGUE.` · `HARUN, MY BROTHER, AS HELPER.` · then, large: `RABBI ISHRAH LI SADRI.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for help with the thing you dread. Settle, and breathe. Name the thing. Put a hand flat on your chest, and notice how tight it is. With each breath in, let your ribs widen a little, as if there were more room in there than you thought. Then ask for one piece at a time. Room inside. An easier task. The right words. And one person you could actually ask to come with you, or text first. If you pray, you can use Musa's words: rabbi ishrah li sadri. The bell holds the time.
Loosen my tongue. Musa's four-part prayer before facing Pharaoh: an open chest, an easy task, clear words, and his brother beside him. Today's word.
Your line: expand my chest. Before the hard thing today, take one wide breath, and ask one real person for help. Day fifty.

howItsDone: Many Muslims recite Musa's prayer from Surah Ta-Ha, rabbi ishrah li sadri, wa yassir li amri, before exams, speeches, interviews and difficult conversations.

fork.setup: you're Musa. you've been told: go to Pharaoh. your chest is tight and your words don't come easily. what do you ask for first?
options: a bigger miracle to show Pharaoh.
fork.reveal: he starts inside: expand my chest. then an easy task, a loosened tongue, and his brother Harun as helper. and he's told: your request is granted.

original.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 20:25: "my Lord, expand my chest for me."

trapdoor: what you thought: Musa had a stutter.
what it means: Musa asks to be made big enough for a hard task: an open chest, an easy path, clear words and a brother beside him.
what a scholar hears: sharh as-sadr, the opening of the chest, is a Qur'anic image for ease and readiness; the burning-coal story explaining the knot is from tafsir, not the text.

notes: 20:25–32 paraphrased, not quoted. The transliteration rabbi ishrah li sadri is widely used; confirm.
The burning-coal story (from tafsir / Isra'iliyyat) is explicitly labeled 'a story people tell'. Confirm the Keeper is comfortable with that framing.
Etymology: English 'vizier' from Arabic wazir (via Turkish). Stated as fact; confirm.
'Wazir, one who carries a burden with you': a common explanation linking wazir to wizr (burden). Confirm.
